title: Edmund and the Confession
premise: When insurance investigator Odile Marchetti receives a confession letter postmarked the day after Edmund Vasseur's funeral, he recognizes the handwriting as his own—a letter he wrote at nineteen and believed destroyed. The confession concerns the drowning of Edmund's sister, Camille, thirty years ago, an accident Odile helped cover up to protect the people who raised him. As Odile reopens the case, he discovers someone in town has been receiving copies of old letters for months, each one nudging the truth toward daylight, and that Edmund's death was no heart attack but a silencing. Following alibis woven three decades ago and clues surfacing with the tide, Odile must choose between protecting the loyal circle that saved his life and exposing the lie that has cost two more lives. In the end, he testifies to what he remembers—photographically, painfully—and the town survives its reckoning, though not unchanged.
about_author: Mirabel Whitlock is a former coastal archivist whose novels are known for their patient, tide-like pacing and characters haunted by what they chose to forget. She writes from a converted boathouse on the northern Atlantic coast, where she keeps every letter she has ever received.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Odile Marchetti, POV. Three days after Edmund Vasseur's funeral, Odile receives a confession letter in handwriting only he could have written—his own, aged thirty years. He remembers writing it at nineteen and watching it burn. The emotional beat is cold dread: the past has learned to mail itself.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Establishing his method: fifteen years of filing the town's secrets as an insurance investigator, invisible by design. He catalogs everyone who knew about Camille Vasseur's drowning. Beat: controlled unease as he realizes his invisibility was always someone else's arrangement.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Odile walks the tidal flats where Camille drowned, finding the shoreline altered by thirty years of storms. A child's rusted locket surfaces near the old pilings. Beat: grief he has never permitted himself, sharpening into resolve to understand who mailed the letter—and why now.

chapters.title: The Widow's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile visits Edmund's widow, Sylvie, ostensibly about the estate. Her ledger shows monthly payments to an unnamed recipient for fifteen years—the same span of Odile's employment. Beat: suspicion curdling; the loyalty that sheltered him may have been purchased.

chapters.title: Alibi, Woven
chapters.summary: Odile reconstructs the night of Camille's death through memory: four teenagers, one storm, one lie agreed upon before dawn. He tests each alibi against what he photographically recalls. Beat: vertigo as his perfect memory reveals gaps that were edited, not forgotten.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. A second envelope arrives containing a page of Sylvie's ledger and a single line: 'He kept filing.' Someone knows Odile's role intimately. Beat: paranoia; the correspondent is close, patient, and wants him to keep digging.

chapters.title: The Harbormaster's Silence
chapters.summary: Odile interviews aging harbormaster Gus Perrin, whose boat log from that night has a torn page. Gus admits he saw lights on the water but was paid to misdate his entry. Beat: pity and anger entwined—survival's price paid in small corruptions.

chapters.title: Sylvie's Version
chapters.summary: Sylvie, POV. Flashback chapters within her account: she married Edmund knowing what he'd done, believing silence was love. She reveals she began mailing the letters after finding Edmund's own confession draft. Beat: tragic tenderness; she wanted the truth out gently, not this way.

chapters.title: Heart Attack, Certified
chapters.summary: Odile obtains Edmund's autopsy summary and finds the certifying doctor was the same man who signed Camille's death certificate thirty years ago. Beat: the machinery of cover-up revealed as generational, professional, almost respectable.

chapters.title: The Fourth Name
chapters.summary: Odile confronts the flaw in his memory: there were five on the beach that night, not four. The fifth name has been redacted even from his recollection—someone taught him to skip it. Beat: horror at discovering his photographic mind was curated by others.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: Odile searches the defunct newspaper office and finds a cache of unsent letters Edmund wrote over decades, each confessing a little more. The final draft names the fifth person. Beat: mounting dread as the name becomes legible at the torn edge.

chapters.title: Father Anselm's Confession
chapters.summary: The town priest, dying, tells Odile he received Camille's own letter the week she died—a letter never delivered because it accused someone the parish depended on. Beat: moral collapse of institutions; duty and love shown as interchangeable currencies.

chapters.title: What Odile Owes
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Flashback to age nineteen: how the town's matriarch, Marguerite Vasseur, took in the orphaned Odile and bound his silence to his survival. Beat: devastating self-recognition—he wasn't loyal; he was owned, and gratitude was the leash.

chapters.title: The Fifth on the Beach
chapters.summary: The torn edge resolves: the fifth person was Marguerite herself, present when Camille died, directing the cover-up to protect her son Edmund. Beat: the architecture of Odile's whole life revealed as a monument to her secret.

chapters.title: Marguerite Receives Him
chapters.summary: Odile visits the ninety-year-old matriarch, who neither denies nor confirms, but asks what he thinks the town can survive knowing. Beat: chilling ambiguity; she remains the most loving and most dangerous person he knows.

chapters.title: Copy Three
chapters.summary: A third letter arrives—addressed this time to the police chief, quoting Odile's confession verbatim. The correspondent is forcing exposure whether Odile cooperates or not. Beat: loss of control; the investigation now investigates him.

chapters.title: Sylvie Disappears
chapters.summary: Sylvie vanishes after telling Odile she mailed nothing since Edmund's funeral—someone else is using her correspondence. Odile finds her car at the tidal flats. Beat: terror; the tide that hid Camille may be asked to hide again.

chapters.title: Low Water
chapters.summary: Searching the flats at extreme low tide, Odile finds Sylvie alive, hiding, and the person behind the letters: Gus Perrin's daughter, who found her father's guilt-suicide note and has been executing his unfinished confession. Beat: grief transmuted into terrible clarity.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Pilings
chapters.summary: Climax. At the pilings, Odile must decide: bury the letters as Marguerite begs, or let them stand. Marguerite's health fails mid-plea; Edmund's death is confirmed as murder by her caretaker protecting her secret. Beat: love against duty at knife-point.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Odile gives a formal statement, reciting thirty years of events with photographic precision, naming everyone including himself. The town holds its breath. Beat: catharsis through exactness; truth spoken plainly at last, at full cost.

chapters.title: Sentences
chapters.summary: Aftermath: indictments fall unevenly—the caretaker charged, Marguerite spared by infirmity, Odile granted leniency for cooperation. Sylvie leaves town; Gus's daughter finds peace. Beat: justice as imperfect arithmetic, survival's price finally itemized.

chapters.title: Edmund and the Confession
chapters.summary: Odile, POV, epilogue. He burns nothing now; instead he donates the letters to the town archive under his own name, ending his invisibility deliberately. On the flats, the tide returns what it took. Beat: quiet redemption—loyalty to truth chosen over loyalty to silence.
